title: Raw images, no filters: Why MySpace fans want it back as relaunch hinted
description: For Monticah Hawkins, a 31-year-old real-estate agent in Atlanta, MySpace wasn't just a website – it was a ritual. "You could be authentic on MySpace,
body: For Monticah Hawkins, a 31-year-old real-estate agent in Atlanta, MySpace wasn't just a website – it was a ritual. "You could be authentic on MySpace," she says. "Upload raw images, no filters. You could have snot coming out your nose and nobody would judge." MySpace, once the world's biggest social network, is flirting with a comeback. Its owners, brothers Tim and Chris Vanderhook, say they plan to relaunch the platform, though no date or product details have been announced. A spokesperson for Viant, which owns MySpace, says the company does not have any updates to share "at this time." But just the idea of a comeback has stirred nostalgia among people who remember the MySpace days of more than 20 years ago as a place where personal pages were messy, loud, and deeply individual. It has also caught the attention of creators like Melissa Kristin, a TikTok star with more than 900,000 followers, who grew up on MySpace and remembers it as a more personal digital space. "It was all very much your own little world, your own corner of the internet," Kristin says. That sense of autonomy shaped how she expresses herself online today, and she believes that a revived MySpace should avoid the algorithmic, pay-to-play dynamics that dominate modern platforms. "It would be best served for personal connection rather than performance," she says. "Just to recapture that high we felt as millennials when we got all the friend requests and comments. It helped us feel connected." MySpace launched in 2003 and quickly became a cultural hub, helping artists like Arctic Monkeys, Adele, and Nicki Minaj find early audiences. But its highly customised pages, auto-playing music, and busy layouts eventually became a liability. Facebook's cleaner, simpler design pulled users away, and MySpace struggled through redesigns and ownership changes before fading from mainstream use. Marketing experts say any comeback will depend on learning from that history. Dr Alexa Fox, a marketing professor at the University of Akron, says the platform was a "first mover" in social media, but one that became too complex for many users. She believes MySpace's original strengths – music, creativity, and personal expression – could still resonate, but only with more accessible design. "It could be more user-friendly, with less coding involved," she says.Alex Mills, a social media strategist who has led campaigns for Spotify and Adobe, says the very thing people are nostalgic for, a feed without algorithms, was also "the thing that killed it." "People still want a feed," Mills says. "They just want a better one than the ones optimising for rage bait." Kevin McClary, head of performance marketing at Gorilla 76, believes MySpace should not try to compete directly with Meta, TikTok, or X. "They can be successful and sustainable even as a niche platform," he says, arguing it should be rooted in 2000s culture. McClary says leaning into MySpace's music identity could be a smart move, from profile songs to 2000s-themed festivals and merchandise. He believes the audience could be broader than former users, with younger generations embracing the early-2000s aesthetics they never experienced firsthand. "You see younger generations now buying old point-and-shoot digital cameras, MP3 players, even film cameras," McClary says. "They clearly have an interest in the past." MySpace could meet users where that trend is growing by becoming a place rooted in a "specific time," he says. He noted that creators making 2000s-style content on other platforms are often at the "mercy" of algorithms. Fox agrees that differentiation is essential. "MySpace shouldn't hang their hat on features other platforms already dominate," Fox says, pointing to Reels and short-form videos. Popular formats can be added, she says, but they should not define the platform. She also sees an opportunity to offer a calmer experience. Today's feeds, she notes, are "algorithmic-driven AI, constantly in your face." A platform where users have more control, or simply feel less overwhelmed, could stand out in a crowded market. For fans like Hawkins and Kristin, the appeal is emotional as much as practical. Both say they would return if MySpace kept its original spirit. For now, its comeback exists mostly as a promise – a reminder of a time when social media felt a little less polished and a lot more personal. "Are you still gonna have that same feeling?" Hawkins says. "Are you still gonna feel like, 'oh my god, somebody loves me?'"

schema.headline: Raw images, no filters: Why MySpace fans want it back as relaunch hinted

title: Rare turtle Rhossi to be flown 5,000 miles home to Gulf of Mexico
description: Rare turtle to be sent back home in 5,000-mile 'incredibly emotional' tripImage caption, Rhossi the sea turtle has to travel thousands of miles by pla
body: Rare turtle to be sent back home in 5,000-mile 'incredibly emotional' tripImage caption, Rhossi the sea turtle has to travel thousands of miles by plane to get homeByChris DeardenBBC WalesA rare turtle that washed up on a Welsh beach is being flown 5,000 miles (8,047km) back home to the Gulf of Mexico.Rhossi the Kemp's ridley sea turtle was found close to death in December 2023, and has been nursed back to health by staff at the Anglesey Sea Zoo.Now, conservationists have begun a carefully co-ordinated operation to fly him across the Atlantic ocean, making sure he does not dry out along the way."For his skin, we use KY Jelly - better known as a sex lubricant - because it's gentle on the eyes," said Matt Davidson, curator of Anglesey Sea Zoo.Image source, Anglesey Sea ZooImage caption, Rhossi being weighed and medically checked before his 5,000-mile journeyIt has taken almost two years to plan, including building a special temperature-controlled crate for him, and co-ordinating complex paperwork across two countries.Rhossi normally lives in the sea, but has to travel out of the water – first by helicopter from Anglesey to London, then by cargo flight to Houston, Texas, USA.It means the journey needs to be completed as quickly as possible, and staff have to be constantly on hand to make sure he does not dry out or dehydrate.Davidson said: "We have to make sure that the shell is really well lubricated, so we spread Vaseline all over to stop it drying out and flaking off."The same for the skin – it's really delicate – and especially the eyes, which both have to be lubricated before he goes into the crate and again just before takeoff, or he will start to peel like someone getting sunburned."But I have had to go to the checkout in a chemist's with about eight tubes of KY Jelly and three tubs of Vaseline and explain what's happening when I get strange looks."Image source, Anglesey Sea ZooImage caption, Rhossi was found, barely alive, on a beach near RhosneigrRhossi got his name because he was found on a beach near Rhosneigr on Anglesey in December 2023 by a dog called Meg, out for a walk with her owner.He was less than two years old and was only just alive, in a state that conservationists call "cold-stunned" from being in much cooler water than his normal habitat.Staff at the Anglesey Sea Zoo believe he lost his way while in warmer seas because of strong winds.They have cared for him over the last two-and-a-half years as he tripled in size and grew from weighing under 1kg (2.2lb) to 21kg (46lbs).Image caption, Frankie Hobro, owner of the Anglesey Sea Zoo says flying to the Gulf of Mexico with Rhossi will be an emotional experienceFrankie Hobro, owner of the Anglesey Sea Zoo, said: "Cold-stunned turtles rarely survive without specialist help - we didn't know if he would make it in the first week or two."Turtles belong in the wild, not in captivity, so it's incredibly emotional because this is what we've been working towards for more than two years."But we have got to know him and his individual quirks while caring for him, and we know that soon, a little piece of us is going to be swimming off into the Caribbean Sea, and we'll never see him again."Image caption, Conservationists hope Rhossi's release to the wild will help the species surviveKemp's ridleys are the rarest sea turtle in the world, and lay their eggs on only two beaches in Mexico and in Texas, USA.The Anglesey Sea Zoo hopes that Rhossi's release back into the wild will be a small step towards the survival of the species.Rhossi is the fourth sea turtle to be rescued and rehabilitated by the zoo over the past decade.Staff are currently planning to build a special turtle rescue centre to care for any more sea turtles found cold-stunned around the Welsh coast.

schema.headline: Rare turtle Rhossi to be flown 5,000 miles home to Gulf of Mexico

title: Burnham to set out cost-of-living measures as he tours UK
description: The prime minister is set to announce "a series of measures to make life easier" for those struggling with the cost of living in the coming days, Down
body: The prime minister is set to announce "a series of measures to make life easier" for those struggling with the cost of living in the coming days, Downing Street says.No 10 says Andy Burnham's plans are to "give people some room to breathe". He will also focus on ways of "improving high streets" as he embarks on a tour of the UK.But the government is facing continued pressure over its early release scheme for prisoners in England and Wales – with criticism of the fact that two of PC Andrew Harper's killers will be eligible from next year.Burnham is also likely to face pressure for more action on the cost of living – although significant interventions are unlikely before October's Budget.Even then, Chancellor John Healey has made it clear he will oversee "strong fiscal discipline" – which will limit how much the government has to spend.The prime minister has been on holiday this week, but Downing Street said he would be in "listening mode" in the coming days as he tours the UK's nations and regions and works on a "10-year plan to bring back hope".A spokesman for the prime minister said: "He thinks Westminster has got used to telling people that everyday hassles – like hidden pricing and consumers being ripped off – must be accepted as part of life. "He doesn't think that's right. That's why he's going to start rolling out a series of pro-consumer cost of living measures to give people some room to breathe."The spokesman added: "He's also going to be kicking off his summer tour around the country, getting out of Westminster and meeting people where they are. "The prime minister is going to be in listening mode to help inform his 10-year plan to bring back hope and make Britain better off."There are, though, likely to be continued questions about the forthcoming early release scheme, due to start in October.One of Burnham's first acts in Downing Street was to order a review which limited the range of people who would be eligible.But those convicted of manslaughter will still qualify for the scheme – including two of the killers of PC Andrew Harper.The prime minister has faced calls from PC Harper's family, former senior police officers and opposition politicians for them to be denied early release.But he has said he cannot go any further without risking prison capacity. Downing Street said on Saturday night that position remained unchanged, despite reports the prime minister could revisit the case.The Conservatives said the government's "tax hikes and red tape are hammering our high streets".Shadow chancellor Mel Stride said: "This is breathtaking hypocrisy from Burnham… they are forcing businesses to close, destroying jobs and driving up prices for the public. "Meanwhile, Labour are plotting to release dangerous criminals onto our streets, leaving people feeling unsafe in their communities."Liberal Democrat Treasury spokeswoman Daisy Cooper said struggling high street businesses "need more than a new PM embarking on a vanity tour this summer".She said the PM should adopt the Lib Dem plan for high streets: "That means reversing the damaging jobs tax, delivering an emergency VAT cut for hospitality, replacing broken business rates and cracking down on the ghost landlords leaving our shop fronts vacant."Reform UK's economic spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "If Andy Burnham wants to help people with the cost of living, he should scrap the green levies and taxes on energy bills and rule out tax rises at the Budget."

schema.headline: Burnham to set out cost-of-living measures as he tours UK

title: Why PC Andrew Harper's death touched so many
description: On the night of 15 August 2019, Lissie Harper got a knock at the door. She thought it was her husband Andrew coming home from work.Instead, it was uni
body: On the night of 15 August 2019, Lissie Harper got a knock at the door. She thought it was her husband Andrew coming home from work.Instead, it was uniformed officers, there to tell her that the man she had married four weeks earlier had been killed while on police duty."Everything I had known in my life to be true was robbed away. Every ounce of beautiful peace, gone," Lissie later said of the moment she was told.They had met as teenagers and were together for 13 years.In her eulogy at his funeral, Lissie recalled how Andrew would pass her notes in class.They were, she said, "true childhood sweethearts, loving one another more and more with each passing day".They had been about to go on their honeymoon.But, on that night nearly seven years ago, everything changed.The case has been back in the headlines because two of PC Harper's killers – Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole – will become eligible to be released early under government plans to tackle prison overcrowding.As the disturbing details of the case are revisited, his family, fellow officers and the public are outraged once more – at what happened, and at the perpetrators' impending release.PC Harper's death was brutal and devastating, causing shock, anger and an outpouring of grief across the country.Pictures of the smiling faces of his teenage killers laughing and joking as they left court only added to that anger.PC Harper had been about to head home at the end of a long shift when he and a colleague were called to reports of a burglary.He was "going beyond the call of duty", the prosecutor at the Old Bailey trial in 2020 said.During the case, haunting dashcam footage from the police patrol car was played showing the moment PC Harper confronted teenagers Henry Long, Bowers and Cole down a dark country lane. He then disappeared from view.His ankles had got caught in a strap trailing behind the car being driven by Long that had been used to tow a stolen quad bike.PC Harper was dragged for over a mile. He died on the road. His police badge and stab vest were found scattered along the route.The three teenagers were tried for murder. In the end, the jury convicted Bowers and Cole of manslaughter. Long had already pleaded guilty to that offence.It meant the jury was not sure that PC Harper's killers knew they were dragging the officer behind the car.But the Judge, Mr Justice Edis, described it as a manslaughter case which was "very close to a case of murder" in its seriousness.Some 6,000 prisoners had been due to be let out early under a law aimed at making space in the prisons system.Burnham paused that policy for a review after a public backlash, with particular focus on the possible release of two of PC Harper's killers after serving half rather than two-thirds of their sentences.But on Monday, while it was confirmed that about 1,000 prisoners would be excluded from the scheme, Bowers and Cole were not among them.Lissie described this as "disgraceful and disgusting", while PC Harper's mother said she was "devastated".A petition against their release has received more than 750,000 signatures.Long, the driver, is not eligible for early release.Recent weeks have shown just how much the case continues to stir strong emotions.Tiffany Lynch, chair of the National Police Federation of England and Wales, said that for rank and file officers up and down the country it "feels personal" – "there is disgust, upset"."We have a police officer who was four weeks into his marriage, dedicated to his job, responding to an incident of burglary, that our public expect of our police, has sacrificed his life in the line of duty and the people are not fulfilling their sentence," she said. "It just doesn't make sense."Stuart Blaik, the senior investigating officer in PC Harper's case, told BBC Breakfast his killers' early release was "particularly hard to understand" and would impact police morale.Justice Secretary Alex Norris has apologised to victims and their families and said the government was trying to avert "a prison capacity crisis".

schema.headline: Why PC Andrew Harper's death touched so many

title: Zainab Jiwa: My viral moment with Zendaya at The Odyssey premiere
description: Zendaya saw me on the red carpet and her jaw dropped - I'm still in shock Image source, Zainab JiwaImage caption, Zendaya's reaction to Zainab's outfi
body: Zendaya saw me on the red carpet and her jaw dropped - I'm still in shock Image source, Zainab JiwaImage caption, Zendaya's reaction to Zainab's outfit got 19m TikTok viewsByNoor NanjiCulture correspondent"I can't zip this! Mummm?"This was 29-year-old Zainab Jiwa, calling out for help squeezing into a corset while filming a "get-ready-with-me" TikTok video. It's a scene many 20-somethings still living at home will relate to.The difference is, Zainab was on her way to the recent London premiere of The Odyssey, one of the summer's biggest blockbusters.She was invited there as a guest and says she caught the eye of Hollywood megastar Zendaya, thanks to her custom look: a striking gold gown complete with a hood."She just walked past, and she saw me there. Her jaw just dropped, so did mine," Zainab tells me."It was just a stare-off for a minute, and she was like, 'Oh my god, amazing, amazing,' and then she just walked off.""I’m still in shock,” she adds. “The thought of her noticing my outfit blew my mind."The interaction went viral, external with 19m TikTok views. Her phone blew up.While Zendaya has been ruling the red carpets with high-fashion "method dressing" – where stars match outfits to a film's themes – Zainab is perhaps proving that independent creators like her can give Hollywood a run for its money.Zainab, who is Muslim and wears a hijab, is also often one of the only people covering her hair at premieres, but she says finding ways to incorporate modest wear is part of the fun."Even though you're covered, you can still find a way to be on theme.”Image source, Dave Benett-WireImage/Getty Images/HBO Max UKArriving for our interview at BBC Broadcasting House this week, her look was on-point in an olive shirt, tie, and brooches. "I put in effort today," she says.She's a self-confessed fashion addict. "From the womb," she says, when I ask her when her passion started.Her other love is film - but she initially kept that as a hobby. Still, she posted videos on social media for fun about her favourite films and outfits inspired by them.Soon, major studios took notice. Disney was first, offering her a junket interview for the series Moon Knight, where she got to interview stars on the red carpet."I thought it was a scam,” she says. “I can’t watch that back. I was NOT good.”Image source, Jeff Spicer/ Getty Images for Sony PicturesToday, Zainab is a full-time creator and presenter, interviewing A-listers like Denzel Washington, Paul Mescal and Tom Hiddleston – while decked head to toe in outfits paying homage to the films.She's one of many digital content creators on the red carpet, with others including Chicken Shop Date’s Amelia Dimoldenberg, Reece Feldman and social media personality Jake Shane.It's not always easy. Sometimes, Zainab gets invites to premieres the night before, meaning a mad rush to sort her look before travelling to the event - often by public transport (“and I look ridiculous”).She works with a range of designers and brands, but says she also keeps costs down by reusing items as much as possible.Her outfits are purposely bold, allowing her to "break the ice" with stars. For House of the Dragon season two, she wore a red gown by a student designer featuring three faces wearing hijabs."I'm a bit extra, but I like to add culture in everything I do," she says.For Spider-Man: Brand New Day, she customised her look with spiderweb henna. For Gladiator II, she wore gold armour.Image source, Simon Ackerman/FilmMagicShe admits she has worried whether dressing modestly will make it harder for her to succeed in this industry, but she finds pleasure in it too."I have a fun time working around the fact that I cover my hair or I cover my arms," she says. "I'd call it halalify the look. I'd always say, ‘'but how do I halalify this?'""I enjoy that bit the most because it shows there's no restriction really here."But while Zainab spends much of her time rubbing shoulders with Hollywood royalty, home life in Harrow, north-west London is completely different."Oh my god, my house is chaos," she laughs. Storage space is at a premium, and outfits often end up "shoved somewhere".She has a cat, siblings who often pop in, and parents who are frequently enlisted for wardrobe emergencies.Despite it not being the career trajectory they’d expected for their daughter, Zainab says her parents are now "so supportive".Image source, Walt Disney Ltd/BAFTA/Paramount Pictures/WireImage via Getty ImagesWith 660,000 followers on TikTok and close to 400,000 on Instagram, she's becoming a key content creator in this field. But she also faces criticism - including from some who claim her outfits are not modest enough."There's always hate in this industry," she says. But she adds: "For every negative comment, there's so many positive ones."If I'm doing it to inspire other people, or entertain other people, or educate other people, if that's still happening, then I really don't care about the rest."For now though, Zainab is swept up in enjoying a string of blockbusters."The summer's felt good for film - I think it's exciting," she says."And there's loads more coming. We've got Dune. We've got Doomsday," she says."I love film and TV. I think it's a really fun way to build community," she adds. "I'm just a fan. At the end of the day, I'm just a fan."

schema.headline: Zainab Jiwa: My viral moment with Zendaya at The Odyssey premiere

title: Youri Tielemans: Man Utd midfielder impresses on debut against PSG
description: The sample size was only 26 minutes.Yet the little combinations between Youri Tielemans and Bruno Fernandes after both were introduced in the second h
body: The sample size was only 26 minutes.Yet the little combinations between Youri Tielemans and Bruno Fernandes after both were introduced in the second half of Manchester United's 1-1 draw with Paris St-Germain in Gothenburg drew an appreciative response from senior figures at the club.With much made of United's activity - or lack of - in the transfer market this summer, it was good timing that Tielemans could make his debut when Mason Mount, arguably the club's player of pre-season, needed to be replaced after just 20 minutes.Head coach Michael Carrick told Norwegian broadcaster VG post-match that Mount had come off as a precaution after taking a hefty blow to his foot. The former Chelsea midfielder walked freely past reporters to the team bus an hour after the final whistle.Nevertheless, Tielemans was a surprise signing when Manchester United triggered a previously unknown £35m clause in the Belgian's contract at Aston Villa to agree a five-year deal.There was a lot of debate in the immediate aftermath about how much football the 29-year-old, who made his professional debut for Anderlecht when he was just 16, had played.It obscured his talent.Against PSG he did not do anything particularly special.There were a couple of 45-yard cross-field passes that found their intended targets. There were some simple first-time lay-offs to team-mates within 10 yards.There was also a short sprint just outside the United area to close down dangerman Khvicha Kvaratskhelia when Tielemans recognised the PSG star could be about to take possession within shooting distance.He got there, won the ball and played a simple pass, taking the ball out of harm's way.This isn't really what got the United contingent purring.They were reacting to the little passes between Tielemans and Fernandes, which allowed United to ease their way out of trouble or move up the pitch.Fernandes was the key man last season as United finished third. Nine goals and 21 assists was a decisive contribution in returning the club to the Champions League after a two-year absence.Tielemans showed in his brief cameo he can take some of the pressure off the Portuguese."Youri has consistently been one of the most outstanding midfielders in the Premier League throughout the past seven years," said director of football Jason Wilcox on Tielemans' signing."He will add further composure, creativity and leadership to our squad."He has all of the technical qualities, as well as the ambition and mentality, to thrive at Manchester United."If Wilcox reflects on those words as United head off to the Republic of Ireland for their week-long training camp in Maynooth, he can be quite pleased with himself.It was only 26 minutes, but on that evidence, he has got it spot on.Carrick has confirmed Marcus Rashford will rejoin the Manchester United squad for their trip to the Republic of Ireland.Rashford, England team-mate Kobbie Mainoo and Argentina defender Lisandro Martinez are the final three players to return for United after the World Cup.Although it was not expected Rashford would return to the club when he joined Barcelona on loan in July 2025, the La Liga champions failed to trigger a £26m option to buy the 28-year-old at the end of the season.Despite interest elsewhere, there has been no deal, meaning Rashford will return to United for the first time since January 2025, when he moved to Aston Villa after falling out with former manager Ruben Amorim.United are training at the plush Carton House hotel in Maynooth and have a friendly with Leeds United at Croke Park on 12 August.They complete their pre-season programme against Amorim's new club AC Milan in Wroclaw on 15 August, when Rashford could make his first United appearance since December 2024 if Carrick decides Wednesday is too soon.A former team-mate, coach and manager of Rashford, it has been felt if anyone can patch up the relationship between club and player - which includes his number 10 shirt being given to Matheus Cunha who is also due to be on the trip after a minor injury ruled him out of the Gothenburg encounter - it is Carrick."I've played with him. I played in the game he made his debut, so we have a history," Carrick said."We have got a full squad this week in Dublin. We fly straight there and have a few days where we have the whole group back together. Marcus is part of that, and Kobbie [Mainoo] and Lisandro [Martinez]. We look forward to seeing them."

schema.headline: Youri Tielemans: Man Utd midfielder impresses on debut against PSG

title: Are the 'luteal uglies' a real thing?
description: "Is it just me or am I the ugliest person alive?" a woman in her early 30s asks the camera on TikTok, accompanied by the caption "POV: Girls in their
body: "Is it just me or am I the ugliest person alive?" a woman in her early 30s asks the camera on TikTok, accompanied by the caption "POV: Girls in their luteal phase."The video has 2.4 million views and hundreds of comments."This is literally me," one woman writes. "I'm angry at how accurate this is," another says.There are thousands of videos like this one on social media, lamenting the "luteal uglies" - the changes in appearance and mood that women say appear during the luteal phase of their menstrual cycle.During this phase, which occurs in the second half of a woman's cycle and ends when she gets her period, women experience a huge drop in oestrogen. So are the "luteal uglies" a real thing?According to Dr Louise Newson, a GP and women's hormones specialist, this change in hormone levels means women can experience a shift in their appearance, sleep and mood during this time. "Our hormones affect our skin, they affect our collagen, so a lot of people find their skin becomes drier, their complexion not so bright, they might have acne and spots," Newson explains. "They might get bloating and breasts can change shape."Elena, who works in hospitality and as an actress in London, says she feels lethargic and "completely unmotivated" during her luteal phase."I feel like my brain is working in slow motion, I tend to become clumsy and way more forgetful," she says. "I don't want to socialise as much and I feel low."Newson says that while women are starting to talk more about the impact of their cycles, many still do not know what to do about it."These women are genuinely suffering and it's affecting their ability to work, function, socialise and just exist," she says.The response to women's concerns can also be frustrating, she adds."Would you say to a man 'Oh your testosterone is down, just don't go to the gym, have a duvet day?' It's unacceptable that women have to put up with it."Your relationships may also change during the luteal phase, Newson says - which is something freelance journalist Henrietta experiences."If I find myself wanting to get irritated with my wonderful, hilarious, chilled out partner there's an extremely high chance I haven't had my coffee, haven't eaten or that I am in my luteal phase," said the 30-year-old.It also affects her friendships. "With my friends, I tend to either overshare and regret it, or isolate myself from them and regret it."More education and discussion about menstrual cycles are needed, says Elena, who only learned about the luteal phase through social media at the age of 24.O'Neill says there is "so little education that women receive about the fundamental aspects of how their bodies work".So much so that many women have turned to TikTok for help. In one video, which has 2.4 million views, a young woman asks: "Ladies, what do you do during your luteal phase to feel better?! I honestly can't cope any more."There are thousands of comments, with one follower suggesting to "wear baggy clothes and avoid the mirror", and another saying "eat chocolate". Another writes that the luteal phase makes her "avoid my husband", while someone else says they cope by watching television "with a bottle of wine".But this advice may actually be detrimental - so what can help women cope with their luteal phase symptoms?Understanding that it's a "predictable, temporary phase" is important, says O'NeillNutrition is key during the luteal phase, she adds - and staying hydrated can help reduce puffinessEasing off salty foods, reducing alcohol intake, and keeping up movement can all help tooSteering clear of processed foods and alcohol will help you avoid increased inflammation, Newson explainsYou should see a health professional if you are particularly struggling during the luteal phase, Newson adds, encouraging women to advocate for themselves"If people don't get what they think is acceptable in the first, second, third, appointment they should go and see someone else. These symptoms don't usually go on their own," she says.

schema.headline: Are the 'luteal uglies' a real thing?

title: What it's like to chase solar eclipses around the world
description: Image source, under_the_lightsImage caption, Mark Griffiths drove from Cheshire to Spain for the eclipse, stopping in France to take picturesByGeorge
body: Image source, under_the_lightsImage caption, Mark Griffiths drove from Cheshire to Spain for the eclipse, stopping in France to take picturesByGeorge SandemanOn Wednesday, parts of Europe will be plunged into daytime darkness as the moon passes in front of the sun, temporarily blocking its light and casting a shadow across the continent.For many of us, it will be a once-in-a-lifetime experience. But for some, following eclipses has become something of an addiction.Armed with two high-spec cameras, a specialist telescope and a drone, Mark Griffiths has spent two days driving from Cheshire to Galicia - one of the best places to view the eclipse - to record the event.It's a hobby that started six years ago, when he went to Shetland to see the northern lights - though the weather was so dreary he "didn't see anything".But it didn't put him off and he soon found he couldn't stop. He loved the thrill of witnessing and capturing the sky's most spectacular events.Image source, under_the_lightsImage caption, The view towards the sky from the hill in Galicia where Mark hopes to capture the total eclipseHe's since filmed the northern lights numerous times - he goes to Iceland once a month and leads tour groups there - and has photographed various auroras, eclipses and bioluminescence.But this is his first total solar eclipse."I kept wanting more," he says, and Europe's first total solar eclipse for more than 25 years is "like what the World Cup is to football" for enthusiasts like him."I'll be honest, it's like an addiction now," he tells me.I'm speaking to him the day after he's finished his marathon drive from England, across France and into Spain. He only paused to take photos of the night sky and rest for a few hours in Bordeaux. "I'm quite sleep deprived."The path of total eclipse begins at the tip of Siberia before curving round the Arctic Ocean and crossing parts of Greenland and Iceland.It then proceeds across a stretch of the northern Atlantic Ocean before reaching northern Spain and finishing in the Mediterranean. Other parts of Europe will see a partial eclipse.The total eclipse is only expected to last a couple of minutes for people who watch it, but that doesn't deter eclipse hunters from crossing continents to witness it.Samantha Phillips-Brown and her husband Gregory have flown to Iceland and hired a camper van so they can drive to a remote area to see it.Image source, Samantha Phillips-BrownImage caption, Samantha and Gregory Phillips-Brown flew from upstate New York to Iceland to see the eclipseThis will be the second solar eclipse they've witnessed.It was the awe-inspiring power of the first one they saw, near their home in upstate New York in 2023, that convinced them to travel for this one. They booked their flights and van more than a year ago."It was such a phenomenal experience to see the Sun start going dark and hear, suddenly, the birds stop chirping," recalls Samantha. "It's just a very strange experience."Gregory thinks of how Iceland's first settlers must have felt witnessing such a phenomena more than a millennium ago, a time of mythological rather than scientific explanation."They really didn't know what was happening, didn't know how long it was going to last... it must have been quite terrifying for them, in a way."They are spending the days before the eclipse driving round eastern parts of Iceland to go hiking and camping.Image source, Samantha Phillips-BrownImage caption, Samantha and Gregory booked their flights and camper van more than a year agoThe path of totality crosses the western part of Iceland and they hope to find a spot in the Westfjords peninsula to witness it.Although they've heard rumours of roads being closed to stop too many people overwhelming the area, so are keen to get there a couple of days before the spectacle.Samantha, who her husband describes as an "obsessive travel planner", is all over the Facebook groups and social media pages being used by eclipse hunters to share information and advice.She's expecting a good turnout given the number of eclipse glasses she's seen people with in Iceland. "They're really trying to prepare everybody," she says."What I expect, as we start inching westward, is we're going to see more and more of them."Andrew Wills is also going to an island to see the eclipse, albeit a much warmer one: Majorca.He's travelling with his wife and his dad, who is 90. Father and son witnessed Europe's last total solar eclipse together in 1999 while stood atop St Agnes Beacon in Cornwall.The landmark, believed by some to be a Bronze Age bowl barrow, offers panoramic views across the Cornish countryside and out to the Atlantic. It was a cloudy day, remembers Andrew."We didn't see the shadow rushing across the sea towards us, though we did see the dawn appearing and it getting closer very quickly," he says. "It was awe-inspiring."Image source, Andrew WillsImage caption, Andrew Wills is travelling to Majorca with his wife and 90-year-old father to see the eclipseHe has high hopes for a clearer day in Majorca where he has booked a villa near the town of Andraitx, located in the west of the island.Andrew has earmarked a spot nearby he hopes will give a good view across the sea. Their location in the path of totality means the eclipse will likely happen low on the horizon."We're going to take a couple of camping chairs with us, so Dad can sit if we can get there an hour or so before."The islands of Majorca and Menorca will be the last places on land to view the eclipse before the Sun sets and the shadow disappears.Eclipses have fascinated Andrew ever since he saw his first in St Agnes all those years ago."We live on a planet where we have this amazing coincidence. Where the Sun is 400 times bigger than the moon but the moon is 400 times closer."And so when the moon passes in front of the Sun and between Earth, it casts this perfect shadow."It made him appreciate the delicacy of life on our planet in the way astronomer Carl Sagan once did when speaking of the Pale Blue Dot photograph."We are tiny little specks in a huge vast area of nothingness," says Andrew. "We're amazingly lucky to be alive."

schema.headline: What it's like to chase solar eclipses around the world

title: Chernobyl evacuee on Welsh family that took him in after disaster
description: Chernobyl disaster evacuee 'forever grateful' to Welsh family who took him inImage source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton Honchanka spent a month
body: Chernobyl disaster evacuee 'forever grateful' to Welsh family who took him inImage source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton Honchanka spent a month in Wales as part of the Chernobyl Lifeline programByOscar EdwardsBBC WalesUpdated 2 August 2026In the summer of 1999, 11-year-old Anton Honchanka was looking to escape his contaminated hometown following history's worst nuclear disaster.His journey would take him from Gomel, Belarus, to a United Kingdom that was experiencing a historic total solar eclipse, a major political reshuffle by Prime Minister Tony Blair, and a music chart dominated by singles such as Livin' La Vida Loca.Anton was one of the children evacuated from Belarus following the 1986 Chernobyl disaster in neighbouring Ukraine, after a reactor at the plant exploded and spewed out radioactive material that would spread across swathes of Europe.Due to radiation, parents in Eastern Europe saw the Chernobyl Children's Lifeline program (CCPL) as vital for their children's health with more than 56,000, external coming to the UK for medical aid and humanitarian support.Thirteen years on since the incident, and with the radiation still hanging in the air, Anton had set off on what he saw then as a "new adventure" thanks to the programme, albeit one "not easy" for his mum to see him leave."My mum was really happy that I had the opportunity to go on the trip," said Anton, now 38."But it wasn't easy for her not having me at home."Anton travelled by bus to Minsk, the capital of Belarus, and from there he flew to the UK.His first clear memory upon arriving in the UK was meeting his first host family. "That's where my experience in Wales really began," he said."My first impression was how peaceful and welcoming everything felt. It had such a cosy atmosphere that I felt comfortable almost straight away."Anton said the architecture was "different" from what he was used to in Belarus, with clean streets and a "warm and cosy atmosphere".His trip came at a time when Belarusian people were living in an increasingly authoritarian state, external, according to the UN Refugee Agency, in a period marked by severe political crackdowns and economic stagnation.Image source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton, centre, stood with Dmitry on his left and the Amoss familyAnton and another boy called Dmitry spent the first two weeks with Angela Davies and her sons. Despite the language barrier, he said they all understood each other "perfectly".They were then taken to Llanharry, Rhondda Cynon Taf, to live with Peter and Linda Amoss.They welcomed the boys into their home with "incredible warmth", said Anton, finding ways to "spoil" and "surprise" them."They often took us shopping because they wanted to treat us," he said."They were always thinking about how they could make us smile."Anton said he naturally became great friends with their kids Gethin and Charlotte spending their time playing outside, riding bikes and enjoying their time together."Those are memories I'll always treasure," he added.Image source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton visited landmarks such as St Fagans National Museum of HistoryFor Anton, returning home meant going "back to normal life" and he was surprised to find that "nothing had really changed".He and Dmitry gradually lost touch as they lived in different cities."When we arrived in Minsk, I got on a bus to Gomel, and he wasn't on it," he added.Now with two sons of his own, Honchanka said Wales and its people have "stayed in my heart forever"."I would really love to see my host families again if I have the opportunity.""During that time, they became very close and dear to me."Image source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton said they became his 'second family' during his time in WalesThis year marked 40 years since the Chernobyl nuclear disaster which caused a reactor to start spewing out radioactive material that would spread across swathes of Europe.Children from Belarus and Ukraine stayed with host families for four-week recuperative breaks. The clean air, untainted food and clean water helped to lower the levels of caesium and other radiation stored in the children's bodies.Gerrie Bayley, 74, from Prestatyn, first joined the CPPL in 2004 taking in two girls from Belarus.She enjoyed the experience so much, it has since "become her life" and she now serves as the chair of the charity's north Wales branch.Image source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Dmitry, in the Liverpool shirt, lost contact with Anton when they returned to BelarusGerrie said the few weeks in the UK made a remarkable difference to their health."They would sleep all the time. They had these big black circles under their eyes. "By the end of the month, they had energy and were eating well. I cannot say how much difference it made."The communities rallied around the program providing second-hand clothing, free dentist appointments and eye tests for the children."They all had treatment they needed. So many stores helped out." she said.Image source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton became great friends with the Amoss kids during his stayLinda Amoss, 71, said the family were vetted to make sure they had a spare bedroom with enough capacity to house Anton and Dmitry"As far as they were concerned we were a second family."They had already been in the country for a couple of weeks and we were the second family for the latter two weeks of their stay."Linda said she was told that any time spent outside of Belarus would "benefit their health"."There were children with incredibly high rates of cancer in certain areas," she added.Image source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton has two sons of his own called Dmitry and DemyanLike Anton, she said the language was something they had to overcome, but it ultimately proved no issue as the boys "just clicked in"."Food was sometimes a bit of an issue, but my cooking isn't the best anyway," she added.Anton joined the family on trips to local landmarks such as St Fagans, Oakwood Theme Park and Garth Hill. "I don't remember them being particularly homesick because everything was sort of just so new and bright for them," said Linda.Image source, Linda AmossImage caption, Peter and Linda Amoss looked after Anton for two weeks during his stay As the four weeks drew to a close, Linda said she understood that the chance of the boys being able to return to the UK was "very slim" due to the demand for places in Ukraine and Belarus.Until now, she had not heard from Anton or Dmitry, but said it would be "extremely brilliant" if they could meet in person again.She also takes great pride in Wales' role in the Chernobyl Children's Lifeline programme."Wales is incredibly hospitable, and I really do love that about our country," she added.

schema.headline: Chernobyl evacuee on Welsh family that took him in after disaster

title: Gloucestershire woman, 97, breaks record for oldest wingwalker
description: Figure caption, BySteve KnibbsGloucestershire and Clara BullockWest of EnglandA 97-year-old woman who suffered a stroke in 2025 has broken the Guinnes
body: Figure caption, BySteve KnibbsGloucestershire and Clara BullockWest of EnglandA 97-year-old woman who suffered a stroke in 2025 has broken the Guinness World Record for being the oldest female wing walker.Betty Bromage, who lives in Cheltenham, broke her own record which was set when she did the same challenge four years ago.Bromage raised funds for the stroke unit at Cheltenham General Hospital – where staff cared for her when she was sick.Speaking about having done six wing walks since the age of 87, she said: "I'd just get bored of life otherwise. I can't drive, I can't see very well and I get a bit frustrated. So, I want to do the things I can do."Image source, Betty BromageImage caption, Betty Bromage says she would be "bored" if she didn't do wingwalksIn August last year, Bromage had a stroke, which still affects her speech."They [the hospital] treated me so well. It affects my words but the rest of me is fine," she said.Image caption, Bromage broke her own record by completing the wingwalkShe added she raises money for charity because it can make a difference - and because she was inspired by some words she read on a hospital wall where she worked as a nurse."It said 'we pass through this world but once, any good we can do, any kindness we can show, do it now, do not defer or neglected, you will not pass this way again'," Bromage said.Image caption, Imogen Sims said it was "amazing" that Bromage was doing the challengeImogen Sims from Cheltenham and Gloucester Hospitals charity said staff were grateful Bromage is raising money for them."To take on such a daring challenge to support our team is amazing," Sims added."Donations will be used for equipment and will make a real difference for patients and staff."Bromage added: "The only problem is getting up on the wing because I'm quite short. Once you're up there, no problem. The fairground is a lot worse."I'll have to think of something when I'm 100 - something special."Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Gloucestershire

title: Bristol artist Banksy's works cost taxpayers nearly £150k
description: Banksy works cost public almost £150,000Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Banksy stencilled a mural on a wall of the Royal Courts of Justice in 202
body: Banksy works cost public almost £150,000Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Banksy stencilled a mural on a wall of the Royal Courts of Justice in 2025ByAnthony WardBristolThree artworks by street artist Banksy have cost taxpayers almost £150,000 in cleaning operations and security so far, with the bill expected to rise.The largest single cost relates to a mural painted on the Royal Courts of Justice in September 2025, where removal efforts and security have so far cost more than £85,000.The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) says it has spent £50,000 trying to remove paint from the wall of the Grade II-listed building in Carey Street. A further £35,300 was spent on overtime and security costs.The spending was disclosed to the BBC through Freedom of Information requests and is likely to reignite debate over whether Banksy's work is vandalism or valuable public art.Banksy, who emerged from Bristol's graffiti scene in the 1990s and became one of the world's most famous street artists, is known for murals and installations that often appear overnight and attract large crowds.The latest costs relate to a mural depicting a judge in a wig battering a protester with his gavel, which appeared on the Royal Courts of Justice in London on 8 September 2025.Banksy claimed the image as his own work, by posting it on his website and Instagram account.Costs mount at Royal CourtsA HM Courts and Tribunals Service (HMCTS) spokesperson said: "The Royal Courts of Justice is a listed building and HMCTS are obliged to maintain its original character."The Metropolitan Police have confirmed: "On Monday, 8 September officers received a report of criminal damage to the side of the Royal Courts of Justice."At this time, no arrests have been made and the investigation remains ongoing."Court staff barricaded off the area and guarded it. Attempts to clean off the mural began immediately.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Security guards screened off the mural and stood guardBut the fact he has painted on an historic court has divided opinion.Shadow Justice Secretary Nick Timothy said: "It's outrageous that tens of thousands of pounds of taxpayers' money – maybe more – will have to be spent cleaning up after Banksy, who seems to believe he has a right to deface public buildings with impunity."Our courts are a national symbol of justice and the rule of law."Banksy's vandalism should be stopped and he should foot the bill for the costs he imposes on others."However, art critic Estelle Lovatt defended Banksy's work and pointed to the benefits for tourism: "Some people visit Buckingham Palace and others visit Banksy's art. "His work brings people together in a way that politics can divide us. He's like the Pied Piper or a town crier. "It can be intimidating if a mural appears on your building, in terms of the crowds, but he makes art accessible because there's no gallery fee."Image caption, Cleaning efforts are continuing behind scaffolding, panelling and a locked doorwayIt's not the first time Banksy has painted on a listed building. His early works in Bristol included a mural of a man hanging from a window, on a Georgian house.First attempts to scrub off the paint on the court were not completely successful, so contractors have been on site using "laser technology". Westminster City Council will have to inspect the wall and if the removal is deemed incomplete, another cleaning method will have to be used.As a final option, the affected stonework may have to be removed and replaced.A Listed Building Consent (LBC) application has been submitted for the installation of railings across the wall that Banksy targeted. If approval is granted then the costs to install the railings are not yet known.Previous works incurred expensesThe court mural is not the first of Banksy's works to create costs for public bodies.In April, a statue of a man carrying a flag appeared in Waterloo Place near Trafalgar Square.The flag covers the man's face and he appears to be about to step and fall from the plinth.Banksy claimed responsibility with a video on Instagram showing the night-time installation.Westminster City Council, which owns the land, says it had no prior knowledge of the statue.The authority said it had spent almost £60,000 on safety barriers, administration and paying for a security guard to keep watch over it.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Westminster City Council has spent £60,000 dealing with the statueIn response to a Freedom of Information request, Westminster Council said: "Ownership of the statue now sits with the council as landowner."The council has notified the artist's agent that it is reviewing options for the short, medium and long term."The BBC has asked for more clarification on this statement.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Banksy painted a Piranha fish on a City of London Police sentry box in 2024In August 2024, Banksy painted piranha fish on a City of London Police sentry box.The sentry box had been installed in the 1990s as part of security measures introduced after IRA attacks in the City of London.After Banksy painted it, the box was removed at a cost of £2,200 and was never replaced.It was put in storage and is due to be displayed at the London Museum when it reopens in November.The works are a reminder of Banksy's continuing influence more than three decades after he first became known in Bristol, where surviving murals remain among the city's best-known tourist attractions.Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in BristolRelated topicsBristolBanksyStreet artStatues and sculpturesGraffitiMetropolitan Police ServiceCity of London PoliceWestminster CouncilLondonCity of LondonArt

title: Poo, parking and poor pitching - the Lake District's summer battles
description: Image source, United UtilitiesImage caption, Lake District authorities say litter, fly-camping and irresponsible behaviour are big problems over the s
body: Image source, United UtilitiesImage caption, Lake District authorities say litter, fly-camping and irresponsible behaviour are big problems over the summer monthsByFederica BedendoNorth East and CumbriaMillions of people visit the Lake District every year, but not all of them abide by the Countryside Code's plea to "leave no trace". It means for enforcement officers and volunteers, summer is often marked by irresponsible parking, inconsiderate camping and even human waste - which doesn't quite have the same ring to it as the Summer of Love."Fifty-plus members of the public engaged with, 10 overnight campers spoken to, eight bags of rubbish collected and they had the joy of seeing one man using a bush as his toilet," reads out Judith Derbyshire, a Westmorland and Furness councillor.It is an extract from a report by patrol officers responsible for tackling anti-social behaviour, who were out in the Coniston area one weekend in July."I'm going to lower the standard of the conversation here but the issue is to do with human poo," says Derbyshire, although she might have used slightly more colourful language.She is responsible for community safety at the Liberal Democrat-led council and says since Covid there has been a surge in visitors who arrive without plans for accommodation, meaning fly-camping is rife.Fly-camping takes place away from designated camp sites and without landowners' permission."Don't feel you can just come up, park up on a lay-by and then go and put a tent up down by the lake shore - you shouldn't be doing that," she says.Image caption, Volunteer litter pickers are often left to deal with the aftermath of fly-campingIt is not just about the litter. Derbyshire says people are also chopping down branches and trees to light fires, causing damage to the environment."There's a tree down at Ullswater, as you're driving down the A592."It's a very large oak tree and somebody fairly recently has put a bonfire up the hollow inside it and, sorry, it's a lovely, big, old oak tree and I want it to be there in a long time to come." Image source, United UtilitiesImage caption, Problems include people chopping down trees to light firesWestmorland and Furness Council and Cumberland Council are responsible for looking after parts of the Unesco World Heritage Site.Together with Cumbria Police, they can enforce Public Spaces Protection Orders (PSPOs), which help tackle anti-social behaviour.It means in areas covered by a PSPO they have extra powers, such as making someone leave the site or issuing a fine.   Derbyshire says Westmorland and Furness officers have only issued eight tickets so far this summer, as enforcement is seen as a last resort.Instead, the authority tries to "engage, educate and encourage"."If we've perhaps gone out and seen a group in the evening and then gone back in the morning and they're not tidying up, they've done damage and they've said they weren't going to have a bonfire and they obviously have and it's still burning, then that gets to the enforcement stage," she says.Image source, Westmorland and Furness CouncilImage caption, Councillor Judith Derbyshire says officers are often left to deal with the mess from fly-campersEnforcement is made difficult by the fact the council has "very few" officers and there is no round-the-clock response service, Derbyshire says."Putting it bluntly, we are going to have strong cutbacks from our funding as a local authority, we're not going to have the staff to be able to put that sort of thing in place."Fines for breaching a PSPO are currently at £100, but Derbyshire says the government is expected to issue new guidance which could see them raise to £500.For irresponsible parking, councils can issue a £50 ticket which is reduced if paid within a certain timeframe."The problem that we've got now is that a parking ticket is not really a deterrent," says Rob Lewis, a senior manager at Cumberland Council's highways department."If there's four or five people in a vehicle, some of them will just share the cost of that ticket and they'll take it as a parking charge - so it's almost part of the expense of the day out."He says the Labour-led council is in talks with the British Parking Association and other authorities to see if higher charges would be more beneficial in areas such as the Lake District National Park.At busy times, he says, buses have had to be cancelled because badly parked cars are not leaving enough room for them to pass.Image source, Nicola MillnerImage caption, A tent surrounded by litter was left by Windermere last year - one example of the fly-camping the area seesLocal social media pages often show cars parked in front of farm gates, passing places and even private fields.Were there to be a medical emergency or a fire, the stakes would be even higher, Lewis says."We do try and educate the visitors before they come to say where it is appropriate to park and where it isn't appropriate to park."To try and ease congestion on the narrow country roads, shuttle buses serve the most popular areas including Buttermere and the Wasdale Valley, and many operators offer free travel to under-16s during the summer.While Cumberland Council has a team of 25 officers issuing parking tickets, they are spread across the whole authority area, from Millom to Carlisle.Lewis says there is more focus on the Lake District at busy times, but not all bad parking can be enforced by the council."It's not that easy, we cannot issue [tickets] unless there's a restriction in place or unless there's a yellow line down there, or it's part of a disc zone, for example."Image source, Wasdale Action Group/A Wasdale LadImage caption, Social media pages often share images of parking problems in the Lake DistrictHe says problem areas can be flagged to the council, but restrictions may take up to a year to come into force, due to the length of time it takes to go through the process and consult with affected residents.The police have powers to deal with certain issues, such as if a vehicle is causing an obstruction.Derbyshire says people can also contact police if they see anyone behaving in a dangerous way, such as lighting a bonfire that is likely to spread to a large area."We're not encouraging people to go and approach people, but more to feed the information back to us," she says.Image source, Nicola MillnerImage caption, Litter is a blight on beauty spots around the lakesDescriptions of people involved and any vehicle registrations would help them track offenders down, Derbyshire says.She believes working together with residents, visitors and bodies such as the National Trust and other landowners is key to getting the situation under control."We want people to come to Lake District and it's good that there's a wider range of people coming here, it's just that we need to get them educated so they know what they can do and what they can't do."Follow BBC Cumbria on X, external, Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external and listen to Radio Cumbria on BBC Sounds. title: Newspaper headlines: 'Top universities cut entry grades' and 'Uefa set for Infantino inquiry'
description: According to the Sunday Telegraph, European football's governing body, Uefa, is considering launching an investigation into Gianni Infantino's conduct
body: According to the Sunday Telegraph, European football's governing body, Uefa, is considering launching an investigation into Gianni Infantino's conduct, external throughout his entire 16 years as a top official at the organisation. The paper reported yesterday that a woman who worked there was paid off after having an alleged relationship with Infantino. A spokesperson for Fifa tells the Telegraph its president "strongly denies the allegations" and that "any insinuation of inappropriate conduct or violation of statutes or regulations is defamatory".Separately, the paper claims Andy Burnham is considering whether to block the early release of prisoners responsible for the death of emergency workers, external – to ensure PC Andrew Harper's killers remain behind bars. The Ministry of Justice is quoted as saying it wanted to block more offenders from getting out sooner – but could not do so "without risking prisons reaching capacity and collapsing".The shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, has penned an article for the Sun on Sunday, warning of what he calls "disaster" unless the early release scheme is halted., external  He argues there's still capacity within the estate – and points to examples of other countries renting prison spaces overseas.The Observer says that while attention has shifted to who is in prison and for how long – just as important is what happens to inmates while they are behind bars, external. It says so-called "Scandi wings", modelled on units in Sweden and Norway, could help solve the prison crisis by improving rehabilitation. The paper highlights what it calls the "striking" results of one such wing in HMP Wandsworth – which comes complete with a piano and plants from the Chelsea flower show."Fury over Royal funeral plan for shamed Andrew" declares the headline on the front of the Mail on Sunday. It says the King's brother, Andrew Mountbatten Windsor,  is due to receive a royal ceremonial funera, externall – despite being stripped of all his titles. The Cabinet Office and Buckingham Palace declined to comment.The Sunday Times reports that elite universities are accepting more applicants with lower grades, external "in an attempt to fill the gap left by an exodus of high paying international students". The paper says there's been a 10 per cent drop in people from overseas studying in the UK.The Times also reveals what it calls a "top secret plan" by Margaret Thatcher's government  to "bomb" Peru with "voraciously hungry moths"., external It says the prime minister gave her initial backing to the idea in the late 1980s as part of a strategy aimed at destroying cocaine crops, and halting the export of the drug to Britain. But the paper says a lack of support from the authorities in Lima meant the scheme never went ahead.

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'Top universities cut entry grades' and 'Uefa set for Infantino inquiry'
